summary: The Hypertext Jeopardy Protocol (HTJP) inverts HTTP's request/response semantics: the client sends an answer and expects the server to reply with a correct question. This document is a humorous April 1 RFC, published as informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8565 is an April 1st joke that reverses who sends HTTP requests and responses. It also points out that deriving a request from a predictable authorized response could reveal credentials.

questions: why is htjp a security risk
subtitle: An April 1st thought experiment reverses HTTP's request and response conventions.

tldr.problem: This April 1st RFC asks what HTTP would look like if clients sent answers and servers returned the questions that would produce them.
tldr.mechanism: An HTJP client sends an HTTP response message; the server replies with an HTTP request that would elicit that response from an appropriate HTTP server.
tldr.outcome: The RFC calls HTJP a pseudo-protocol using alternative HTTP conventions. It warns that predictable authorized responses could expose credentials and notes that intermediaries do not support the scheme.

today: RFC 8565 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2019. It describes HTJP as an alternative set of HTTP conventions and warns about credential exposure from predictable responses.

sections.title: Reversing HTTP Conventions
sections.content: In HTTP, a client conventionally sends a request and a server sends a response. HTJP reverses these roles: the client sends an HTTP response message, and the server returns an HTTP request that would elicit that response from the appropriate HTTP server. The RFC calls this a pseudo-protocol because the messages remain HTTP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends what looks like a normal HTTP answer. The server works backward and sends the request that could produce that answer.

sections.title: HTJP Messages and Intermediaries
sections.content: An HTJP request must be an HTTP response. Its reply must be an HTTP request that would produce that response if sent to the appropriate server. RFC 8565 says that proxy and cache support for HTJP is not widespread and recommends against deploying it behind such intermediaries.
sections.plainLanguage: The response to an HTJP message is a request that could have produced it. Ordinary proxies and caches may not handle this reversed convention.

sections.title: The Credential Exposure Risk
sections.content: If an authorized HTTP response is predictable, an HTJP server that receives it could return the request that produced it, including credentials, tokens, cookies, or other authorization material. The RFC describes an Anti-HTJP-Nonce response header as a possible defense: its value should be a cryptographically secure random number.
sections.plainLanguage: A predictable answer to an authorized request may let HTJP reveal the original request and its credentials. The RFC suggests adding a random response value to make the answer less predictable.

sections.title: An Informational Thought Experiment
sections.content: RFC 8565 presents HTJP in an April 1st document. It notes that HTTP intermediaries generally expect conventional request and response roles and says they do not broadly support HTJP. Its discussion examines HTTP semantics and security through the reversed-message idea.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an April 1st thought experiment, not a recommended deployment. Its reversal is used to explore how HTTP messages and conventions work.
